body.text: On September 3, 2026, S. Jaishankar ended the first standalone visit ever made by an Indian External Affairs Minister to Ukraine by paying homage to Gandhi at the National Botanical Garden in Kyiv, on a day when Russia had sent its jet-powered Shahed drones towards the city while he was in it. Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who had received him earlier that day, offered a judgment of India warmer than anything Kyiv had said since he called Modi’s embrace of Putin in Moscow in July 2024 a huge disappointment: “This certainly must not be a time of war. Peace is needed. This is India’s clear position.” Jaishankar went on to Warsaw, which was itself a message, and he had come to Kyiv only days after Narendra Modi told Vladimir Putin in Bishkek, with cameras running, that “endless war must now give way to an end of war”.

A month later, the two belligerents said something remarkably similar about India within a day of each other. On October 1, at the Valdai Club in Moscow, Putin said that Modi raised the war at every meeting and had “very good ideas aimed at finding mutually acceptable solutions”, and on October 2, Andrii Sybiha, Ukraine’s foreign minister, told reporters that Kyiv had four truce proposals before it, from India, Turkey, Egypt and the US, and that “the broadest one is India’s proposal”.

This is an odd place for India to be standing, because a year earlier, it had been cast as the war’s paymaster. In August 2025, Peter Navarro, the White House trade adviser, called the conflict “Modi’s war”, Washington doubled its tariffs on Indian goods to fifty per cent as punishment for India’s purchases of Russian oil, and the European Union had already sanctioned the Rosneft-owned Nayara refinery in Gujarat. Nevertheless, irony again died a thousand deaths with the US’ decision to buy diesel from Russia. Here, we are not getting into the details of the high politics of the current negotiations, as the situation is changing rapidly; however, history offers important lessons for India as a “facilitator” in the negotiations. It is also a case in point how values, interests, ideology, and coercion all play a part for a country involved in facilitating the peace process, so in a way it is choosing a battle in itself.

How a country accused of fuelling a war came to be trusted with ideas for ending it has a history, and part of that history lies in the files of a commission India chaired in Korea 73 years ago, seated between Poland and Czechoslovakia on one side and Sweden and Switzerland on the other.
II

By the spring of 1952, the negotiators at Panmunjom had settled almost everything an armistice in Korea required except what to do with prisoners who did not want to go home. Tens of thousands of Chinese and North Korean prisoners held by the United Nations Command refused to return, Washington would not send them back by force, and Beijing and Pyongyang insisted on the return of every man, treating the refusals as the work of the camps’ anti-communist bosses. The war went on for more than a year over this point alone.

The formula that eventually broke the deadlock was India’s. A resolution steered through the General Assembly by V.K. Krishna Menon in December 1952 proposed that prisoners who refused repatriation be handed to a commission of neutral states, and after Stalin’s death in March 1953, the communist side came back to the idea. The agreement on prisoners, signed on June 8, 1953, named five countries to the commission: Sweden and Switzerland, nominated by the United Nations Command; Poland and Czechoslovakia, nominated by the Chinese and North Korean Command; and India, which would chair the commission, serve as its executive agent and provide the only troops. Nehru accepted the proposal from London three days later, telling Beijing that India “would be glad to place their services at the disposal of parties concerned to further the cause of peace in Korea”, provided that the parties gave “full assurances of their cooperation”.

The mandate was a timetable. The Neutral Nations Repatriation Commission, with Lieutenant General K.S. Thimayya in the chair and Major General S.P.P. Thorat commanding the Custodial Force, began taking custody on September 10, 1953, and by September 24 held 22,604 prisoners from the southern side and 359 from the northern side, among them Americans, a Briton, and South Koreans. They were held in two camps inside the demilitarised zone, one on each side of the line, the Southern Camp divided into 6 enclosures and 55 compounds that were run, in practice, by the prisoners’ own leaders, and the Northern Camp at Songgong-ni, with Indian troops guarding both. Each side would then have 90 days to “explain” to its own men why they should come home. The cases of those still unwilling would go to a political conference within 30 days, the remaining prisoners would be declared civilians on the 120th day, and those who wanted to settle in neutral countries would be helped to do so before the commission dissolved itself. Every stage depended on the one before it, and on the two Commands keeping their word.
III

The timetable broke within weeks. On October 19, 1953, after the Custodial Force made it clear that it would not drive unwilling North Korean prisoners into the explanation tents by force, the Polish and Czechoslovak delegates walked out of the commission, and the commission’s own minutes recorded that “certain members of the Commission felt that it constituted such a violation of the Terms of Reference and the Rules of Procedure that they deemed it necessary to withdraw from the meeting”. Nehru backed Thimayya through a cable two days later, but not without conceding the other side its point, “We agree with you in step you have taken although there is some force in objections raised by Czechs and Poles”, and in the same cable he turned on the prisoners’ leaders in the southern camp, who were keeping men from the tents, “This is as much exercise of coercion as anything else.” To his sister Vijayalakshmi Pandit, he wrote more plainly that “the Korean situation becomes more and more difficult and intricate. Thimayya is facing up to it pretty well though I cannot say how far he will succeed.”

He did not entirely succeed. The explanations ran for 10 days out of the 90; gangs inside the camps beat and in some cases, murdered prisoners who asked to go home, and the commission recorded that it had itself been “subjected to a regime of threats and intimidations by the Republic of Korea”. Yet the more revealing story in the files is how India voted when the commission split, because it did not vote with the same partners twice.

The first question, on December 24, was whether the 90 days could be extended. Poland and Czechoslovakia said yes, since the communist side had lost most of its time, but India held that only the two Commands that had signed the agreement could extend it, and voted with Sweden and Switzerland to close the explanations. The second, the same day, was the commission’s interim report, which blamed the prisoners’ organisations and South Korean interference for the failure, and here India voted with Poland and Czechoslovakia, while the Swedish member objected that “it is impossible through such a report to avoid blaming one side or the other”. The third came in January, when Sweden proposed that the remaining prisoners simply be declared civilians on the 120th day. India voted against it with the Poles and Czechs, because the agreement required a political conference to consider their cases first, and when the Swedish member appealed to the Geneva Convention, India’s delegate replied that “you cannot approbate and reprobate at the same time”, a lawyer’s way of saying that no one can claim the rights of an agreement while setting aside its obligations.

India was now alone, and Nehru knew it. “Both sections in Commission may oppose our proposals,” he cabled Thimayya on January 14, “for different reasons, placing us in a minority of one and forced to take executive action.” He had set out the reasoning on Christmas Day: “We are not entitled to ‘release’ prisoners anyhow and would not like the onus of breaches of agreement or allegations of same”, and the only lawful course left was to march the prisoners to the line, “hand them over and obtain receipts”. On January 20 and 21, the Custodial Force returned 21,805 men to the United Nations Command, and Thimayya had told both Commands that he was doing so because “I can neither retain custody of prisoners of war nor further implement the Terms of Reference nor release them.”

Read together, the votes describe a method rather than a tilt. India sided with Warsaw and Prague on what the prisoners were owed, which was a fair hearing and a political conference before any change in their status, and with Stockholm and Bern on what the commission was entitled to do without the consent of the two sides, which was very little.
IV

This method satisfied nobody, and the archive records the dissatisfaction from every direction. Washington had marked the limits of India’s role before the commission even met, in an aide-memoire to Bern in June 1953 which said that India, apart from its executive duties, “will be merely the fifth member of the Commission”, and that “the United States does not consider that India is to be an umpire between the other members”. By October John Foster Dulles was speaking of the “so-called” Repatriation Commission, South Korean newspapers were printing cartoons of Indian soldiers, and Nehru addressed both in a speech in Bombay: “When we are doing our work sincerely and trying to carry out our responsibilities we are described as ‘so-called neutral nations’’’. He added that “nor can anybody accuse Sweden and Switzerland to be pro-Communist, if that be the case with Poland and Czechoslovakia. If anybody thinks we are partisans in this dispute, he is absolutely wrong.”

The handback in January brought the criticism from the other side. Beijing was, in Nehru’s words, “very upset over restoration of POWs” and would have preferred the prisoners to break out of the camps, and he cabled Thimayya that “we cannot agree to these anarchic procedures. We regret Chinese reaction though we understand it.” The United Nations Command said the early return of the prisoners “can only be regarded as a failure” of the commission. At the last meeting, on February 18, 1954, the Polish delegate told the room that “the Indian delegation cannot, therefore, escape part of the responsibility” for the terror in the camps and called the handback “the arbitrary decision” of India, while the Swedish alternate complained of “unilateral acts of the Chairman”, and the Chinese and North Korean Command wrote that whoever inspired the dissolution “will have to answer to history”.

Yet the same files show each of these capitals relying on India in practice. Both Commands had invited it. In November 1953, the Americans floated the idea of seating Thimayya as an observer at the political conference, the Swedes and Swiss accepted the handback “on humanitarian and practical grounds” even while objecting to the way it was done, and the United Nations Command, having called the return of the prisoners a failure, approved Thimayya’s decision to take the 88 men who refused both sides to India. Nehru had anticipated this double attitude in Bombay, when he told his audience that “we should not think that if anybody does not support us he is our enemy”, which is as close as the record comes to a statement of how India read the world in 1953.

The four European states around Thimayya’s table were never neutral in the same sense. Sweden and Switzerland were neutrals by long tradition, while Poland and Czechoslovakia were states whose sovereignty was limited by Moscow, and Polish documents later published by the Wilson Center show the Polish delegates taking their cues on repatriation from Chinese officials. Seventy years on, all four have moved in the same direction. Poland, the Czech Republic and Slovakia joined NATO and the European Union after regaining their sovereignty, and Poland now treats Russia as a threat to its existence. Sweden gave up two centuries of non-alignment and joined NATO in March 2024, the sharpest break of all from its role in 1953. Switzerland remains outside both, but it adopted the Union’s sanctions on Russia in 2022 and has joined the European Sky Shield air-defence initiative, so that its neutrality is now practised inside a Western posture rather than between two camps.

The convergence goes beyond Ukraine. The four share a reading of Russia as the main danger to European security, a commitment to the transatlantic tie and the European sanctions regime, and a growing caution about China, and the dissent that exists, in Robert Fico’s Slovakia and more mildly in Andrej Babiš’s Czechia, is dissent inside the same institutions rather than a different posture.
India is the one member of the 1953 commission that did not converge, though its way of standing apart has changed.

Nehru’s non-alignment meant staying out of blocs; today’s multi-alignment means being part of several groupings at once. India is a member of the Quad with the US, Japan and Australia, the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation and BRICS, whose summit it hosted in New Delhi in September. It has also concluded a free trade agreement and a Security and Defence Partnership with the European Union in January, while refusing to give up its defence and energy ties with Russia.

Part of the difference is a matter of size, because the four Europeans were small powers who, under pressure, sought the security of an alliance, whereas India was weak in 1953 but already claimed a standing of its own, and today has the economic and military weight to sustain the claim.

The archive obviously signals that it’s an old, time-tested policy under a new name. Choosing partners issue by issue, as India did on the commission, is what Indian officials now call multi-alignment, and in 1953, as now, it rested on a reading of international politics in which India counted as a pole of its own and not as an annexe to anybody’s bloc.
VI

The archive also shows that India’s caution was practised rather than preached. Nehru accepted the chair on the presumption that both Commands would give “full assurances of their cooperation”, the Custodial Force refused to drive prisoners into the explanation tents by force even when Warsaw and Prague accused it of letting the camp leaders win, and India would neither extend the explanations nor release the prisoners without the consent of both sides, because, as Nehru cabled, “we are not entitled to ‘release’ prisoners anyhow”. When it handed them back, it did so as prisoners of war, against receipts, so that nobody could say India had decided their status on its own; and even the voyage home was weighed, Nehru told Thimayya that “it is better to avoid American ships”.

The same habits have run through India’s Ukraine diplomacy since 2022. It has offered no tailored plan. Jaishankar said in Kyiv that resolving the conflict was up to the countries involved. India’s proposal focuses on areas where both sides could agree, such as energy infrastructure and safe passage through the Black Sea, leaving territorial questions and security guarantees to negotiations.

Even on oil, where its purchases have risen and fallen with sanctions and with the disruption in the Strait of Hormuz, India has been consistent in principle, refusing to join sanctions or condemn Russia by name while affirming, as Modi did in Kyiv in 2024, that sovereignty and territorial integrity must be respected, and the European Union concluded its trade and defence agreements with India while the tankers were still arriving.

India’s commitment towards the cause also outlasted the commission in 1953. The 88 men India brought home were housed in the Delhi Cantonment, and Nehru told Parliament in March 1954 that most of them were young, that “the largest group consists of students”, and that there were “some doctors, engineers, tradesmen, technicians and farm labourers” among them. When they learnt that the Indians were leaving Korea, some of them had been “much agitated that they might be left behind”, telling the Indians, “We won’t be safe here if you go away”; and Nehru’s explanation for bringing them was simply that “we could not very well leave them in the lurch”. In September 1955, India was still caring for 82 of them, still waiting for the United Nations Command to pay the rest of its share of the commission’s costs, and telling the General Assembly that “the Government of India cannot continue indefinitely to shoulder this burden”.

There is one sentence in the commission’s papers that speaks for all five members. On December 28, 1953, in a week when they agreed on almost nothing, Thimayya sent the interim report to the two Commands with “a hope, shared by all other members of the Commission”, that they would give “earnest consideration to the problem of disposition of the prisoners of war in a manner consistent with the fundamental objectives” of the agreement. The Swedes and Swiss would not endorse the report it accompanied, and the Poles and Czechs would soon call India’s decisions illegal, yet each of them shared that hope. The governments that succeeded those delegations, in Warsaw, Prague, Bratislava, Stockholm and Bern, differ with New Delhi, some of them sharply, about Russia, sanctions and oil, but each of them says it wants this war to end, and that is the hope India carried from Kyiv to Warsaw in September, the one thing that, as in December 1953, everyone at the table can share.

Harsh Pandey is a PhD Candidate in the Centre for European Studies, School of International Studies, Jawaharlal Nehru University, New Delhi. He is also a Visiting Fellow at the Delhi-based Centre for Peace Studies.
